back-side, opp. to פָּנִים and קֶדֶם. Ez.
2, 10 and it (the roll) was written פָּנִים
וְאָחוֹר in front and on the back, i. e. with-
in and without. 1 Chr. 19, 10. Ps. 139, 5.
—Also backward, Gen. 49, 17 וַיִּפֹּל רֹכְבוֹ
אָחוֹר and his rider falleth backward.
Jer. 15, 6. Often pleonast. after verbs
of turning or going away, i. e. of turning
35, 4. 40, 15; and so others. e) Plur.
אֲחֹרִים the hinder parts, the back sides,
2. the west, the western quarter; since
the Hebrew, in speaking of the points of
the compass, always regarded himself as
looking towards the east. Job 23, 7. 8.
Is. 9, 11 וּפְלִשְׁתִּים מֵאָחוֹר and the Philis-
tines behind, i. e. in the west. Comp.
קֶדֶם, יָמִין, תֵּימָן, שְׂמֹאל; also C. B. Mi-
chælis Diss. de locorum differentia rati-
one anticæ, posticæ, dextræ, sinistræ,
Halæ 1735; reprinted in Pott’s Sylloge
Commentt. V. p. 80 sq. § 8.—The Hin-
dus, Mogols, and Irish, follow the same
method.
3. after-time, the future, לְאָחוֹר here-
אָחוֹת f. (for אֲחֹוֶת, from masc. אָחוּ,
which in Arab. and Chald. is i. q. אָחִי)
plur. c. suff. אֲחוֹתַיִךְ Ez. 16, 55 from a
sing. אָחָה, also אַחְיוֹתֵךְ Ez. 16, 52 from
a sing. אַחְיָה, which comes from masc.
אֲחִי; comp. Lehrg. p. 602.
1. a sister, Arab. أُخْتٌ, Syr. ܚܳܬܳܐ for
ܐܰܚܳܬܳܐ, Chald. אֲחָת, id. Pr. a sister of
full blood, i. e. of both the same father
and mother; but spoken also less accu-
rately of a half-sister, e. g. one born to
the same father but of a different mother,
ὁμοπατρία, Gen. 20, 12. 2 Sam. 13, 2. 5;
or one born of the same mother by a
different father, ὁμομητρία, Lev. 18, 9.
11. 20, 17.—The word sister is also em-
ployed by the Hebrews in other and
wider senses; e. g.
2. a relative, kinswoman, Job 42, 11.
So Gen. 24, 60, where the mother and
brother say to Rebecca, אֲחֹתֵנוּ אַתְּ thou
art our sister.
3. a countrywoman, one of the same
tribe or country, popularis, Num. 25, 18.
4. an ally, a confederate city or state,
5. After אִשָּׁה, one—the other, spoken
also of inanimate things of the fem. gen-
der. Ex. 26, 3 five curtains were coupled
אִשָּׁה אֶל־אֲחֹתָהּ one to another. v. 5. 6. 17.
6. Metaph. sister is said of any thing
with which we are intimately connect-
ed; Prov. 7, 4 say unto wisdom, Thou
art my sister. Job 17, 14. Comp. other
words expressing relationship, espec. אָב
no. 8. אָח no. 8.
7. As a term of endearment addressed
to a spouse, Cant. 4, 9 sq. Comp. Tibull.
* אָחַז fut. יֹאחֵז, rarely יֶאֱחֹז 1 K. 6,
1. to lay hold of, to take, to seize, espec.
with the hand. Arab. أَخَذَ, Chald. and
Syr. אֲחַד, ܐܶܚܰܕ. Constr. with acc. of
pers. or thing, Ps. 56, 1. Judg. 12, 6;
often also c. בְּ, Ex. 4, 4. Job 23, 11. 2 Sam.
20, 9 and the right hand of Joab took
hold of Amasa’s beard.—Metaph. ascrib-
ed also to terror, fear, (like λαμβάνειν,)
Ex. 15, 14 חִיל אָחַז יֹשְׁבֵי פְּלָשֶׁת terror
hath taken hold on the inhabitants of
Philistia. v. 15. Ps. 48, 7. But also vice
versa one is said as in Engl. to take
fright, i. q. to be affrighted; Job 18, 20
קַדְמוֹנִים אָחֲזוּ שָׂעַר the ancient ones took
fright, were affrighted, for: ‘ terror seiz-
ed upon them.’ 21, 6. Is. 13, 8 צִירִים
וַחֲבָלִים יֹאחֵזוּן they (the Babylonians)
take hold of pangs and sorrows, for:
‘pangs and sorrows seize upon them.’
2. to take, to catch, e. g. in hunting,
fishing, Cant. 2, 15.
3. to hold, to hold fast that which one
has taken hold of, c. acc. 1 Chr. 13, 9.
2 Chr. 25, 5; בְּ Gen. 25, 26. Metaph.
c. acc. Job 17, 9, comp. κρατέω Rev. 2,
25; c. בְּ Job 23, 11. Part. pass. with
active signif. Cant. 3, 8 אֲחֻזֵי־חֶרֶב hold-
ing the sword. Comp. on this deponent
use of passive participles, Lehrg. p. 309,
310. Heb. Gram. § 49. n. 2; also comp.
for this same verb Syr. ܐܰܚܺܝܕ holding
Ethiop. እኁዝ ehûz, taken, held, also
holding.
4. to hold or fasten together, to join,
and in Pass. to be joined, to adhere.
Many verbs of taking and holding thus
pass over to the notion of joining and

line_status.note: The printed word has no yod between het and vav (contrast line 4, אַחְיוֹתֵךְ, which does), so B is wrong; but A misplaces the pointing — the image shows hateph-patah under the alef and no shewa under the het: אֲחוֹתַיִךְ.

The word after "sing." is printed with only three letters, אָחָה (qamets under aleph and chet, final he); there is no yod or shva as in Reading B's אָחְיָה. The rest of the line (אַחְיוֹתֵךְ, "Ez. 16, 52 from") is identical in both readings and matches the print.
Under the aleph the print shows a hataf-patah (shewa dots plus a short dash), not a plain qamets; the same hataf-patah appears on אֲחִיָה in line 1. A space is printed before the semicolon.
Printed line has a space before the colon ("for :", matching the same spacing at end of line 4) and a space after the opening quote ("‘ terror"); Reading B omits both.

The only difference is the space A puts after the opening quote mark. The gap between ‘ and p in the print is just the normal side-bearing of a raised quote glyph, not a word space (compare it to the real spaces between words on the line), so B is correct: ‘pangs with no intervening space.
